results.title: Telangana Farmers Turn to Cheap Urea as Fertiliser Price Gap Widens
results.description:
HYDERABAD: Agriculture minister Tummala Nageswara Rao said the wide price gap between fertilisers was encouraging farmers to use cheaper urea in excess, affecting soil health and potentially reducing crop quality. He said the prices of urea, diammonium phosphate (DAP) and complex fertilisers should be rationalised to encourage farmers to use nutrients in the recommended balance. [...]HYDERABAD: Agriculture minister Tummala Nageswara Rao said the wide price gap between fertilisers was encouraging farmers to use cheaper urea in excess, affecting soil health and potentially reducing crop quality. He said the prices of urea, diammonium phosphate (DAP) and complex fertilisers should be rationalised to encourage farmers to use nutrients in the recommended balance.

Urea use rises as price gap widens

Urea consumption in Telangana has increased from 14 lakh metric tonnes in 2015-16 to 20.70 lakh metric tonnes in 2025-26. Tummala attributed the rise partly to higher subsidies on urea and DAP. The current nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium (NPK) consumption ratio in Telangana stands at 12.6:4.8:1, against the recommended ratio of 4:2:1. A 45kg bag of urea costs about ₹240-266, while a 50kg bag of DAP costs ₹1,350 and a bag of 19:9:19 complex fertiliser costs ₹1,750. Tummala said the price gap was encouraging farmers to use more urea and DAP while ignoring the balanced nutrient needs of crops.

Excess urea threatens soil, crop quality

In paddy, farmers are using phosphorus and nitrogen above recommended levels. In maize, they use five to 10 bags of urea instead of the recommended three. Cotton farmers are using 10-15% more nitrogen than recommended, while potash use is about 30% lower, officials found. Such imbalanced fertiliser use can cause micronutrient deficiencies, including zinc and boron. It can also increase nitrogen leaching, leading to soil and water pollution. The imbalance may also increase pest and disease incidence, raising cultivation costs for farmers. Tummala said excessive urea use could affect soil health as well as crop quality. He stressed the need for balanced fertiliser use to protect the quality of Indian farm produce and its demand in international markets.

Minister seeks fertiliser price rationalisation

Tummala said the Centre should narrow the price gap between urea, DAP and complex fertilisers and rationalise the pricing policy to promote balanced nutrient use. He said the state government had repeatedly urged the Centre to act, but no visible corrective measures had been taken. The minister also called for steps to curb excessive urea use. He said it was contradictory to promote natural and organic farming while leaving the fertiliser price gap unchanged. Farmers naturally tend to choose urea because it is much cheaper than other fertilisers, he said. This could damage soil health and affect crop quality. Tummala said the Centre had a responsibility to bring balance to fertiliser pricing in the interest of farmers. Merely asking farmers to reduce urea use without changing the pricing structure would not produce the desired results, he said. He urged the Centre to take immediate steps to rationalise fertiliser prices and protect soil health and crop quality.

Farmers urged to follow recommended doses

Tummala directed agriculture officials to ensure that farmers use fertilisers only in quantities recommended by scientists. He also advised farmers to use alternative nutrient sources such as farmyard manure, green manure, vermicompost and biofertilisers. Nano urea and nano DAP could also be used as alternatives to conventional urea and DAP as part of recommended fertiliser doses, he said.

Rythu Nestham to spread awareness

Following Tummala's directions, the agriculture department is using the Rythu Nestham programme to educate farmers on balanced fertiliser use and the risks of excessive urea application. During the 104th episode of Rythu Nestham held on Tuesday, scientists guided farmers on fertiliser use, nano urea and related issues. The Centre has introduced the Fertilizer Sale App (FFS App) to facilitate fertiliser sales to farmers. Tummala directed agriculture officials to create wider awareness about the system at the field level. The app is currently being used for fertiliser sales in 22 districts. Officials are taking steps to extend the service to the remaining districts from August 27. Tummala directed officials to coordinate with nodal officers appointed by the Centre and resolve problems faced by farmers on the FFS App promptly. He also asked officials to regularly educate farmers about fertiliser availability, application methods and the importance of balanced nutrient use. ]]>

results.title: India’s data centre boom: Mumbai cracks global top 15, Hyderabad pipeline set to surge 15x
results.description: Mumbai is ranked 15th globally in operational data centre capacity and 11th in terms of development pipeline, while Hyderabad is placed 27th and 19th, respectively, according to the Knight Frank Global Data Centre Atlas 2026. The report, which compares as many as 36 major data centre markets across North America, Europe, Asia-Pacific, the Middle East and Africa, comes as the rapid adoption of cloud computing and artificial intelligence drives a fresh wave of investment in digital infrastructure.
